summary:
Mari El is a republic of the Russian Federation and stands under Russia's national framework, which presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors. Russia banned legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents was signed; the Supreme Court designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression including anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

The UK government country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the framework under which this division operates. Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition is punishable under the gay propaganda law by fines or detention of up to 15 days, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were affected by enforcement of anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023.

Federal extremism enforcement applies nationwide, Mari El included. Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its alleged symbols, with charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes. The same report records 81 people convicted across 98 court cases since January 2024 for administrative offences involving those symbols, mostly for posts on social media. The 2023 Supreme Court designation that enabled these prosecutions carries penalties of up to 12 years in prison and builds on the 2013 gay propaganda law.

Enforcement is rising in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two years preceding. The Guardian reported on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion and death in custody are documented. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. BBC Russian reported on 27 July 2024 that a transgender woman was lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Mari El has no separate legal regime on gender identity: the criminal, administrative and document rules above apply in full, and no source in this inventory records Mari El-specific enforcement statistics, local prosecutions or incidents of anti-trans violence.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern predates the current crackdown. The propaganda framework originates in the 2013 law, which the 2023 extremism designation converted into a vehicle for criminal charges carrying up to 12 years; the trend line over a decade shows case volume growing eighteenfold rather than stabilising.

Raids on venues have been carried out by masked police in the capital and in at least two other venues in a single night, indicating coordinated operations rather than isolated local initiatives. Charges for displaying alleged extremist symbols have been brought mostly over social media posts, so conduct that is not visible to anyone physically present can still generate a court case.

The scale of harm is measurable: at least 139 people affected by anti-LGBT+ enforcement between 2022 and 2024, 101 extremism convictions recorded as of 30 June 2025, 81 people convicted across 98 administrative cases since January 2024, and more than 60 million rubles collected in propaganda fines over two years.

Conditions inside Russia are compared in the assessment machinery of other states: the UK Home Office treats LGBT+ Russians, including residents of the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as members of a particular social group for refugee purposes, and Human Rights Watch has asked governments to offer safe haven to people leaving the country.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care are unavailable to Mari El residents: the 2023 law bars both gender reassignment surgery and changes of gender marker on official documents, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year.

Same-sex marriage is prohibited and the constitution provides no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people, so residents have no domestic constitutional route to challenge discrimination. Same-sex sexual activity itself is not criminalised.

Residents face administrative fines or detention of up to 15 days for a first propaganda-law offence, criminal prosecution and up to four years' imprisonment for repeat offences, and up to 12 years for extremism charges. Administrative convictions for displaying alleged extremist symbols have been issued in 98 court cases against 81 people since January 2024, mostly for social media content.

Describing LGBT+ life under the current regime, The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, quoting a St Petersburg queer woman who called herself "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.
